The certificate is structured around four required courses that collectively emphasize how planners understand communities, analyze conditions, design interventions, and operate within institutional and legal frameworks.

This course provides critical perspective on the social, political, and ethical dimensions of planning.
The Introduction to Planning Methods course focuses on the analytical and technical tools used by planners to assess community conditions, support decision-making, and evaluate planning outcomes.

Students develop foundational skills in planning analysis and learn how methods inform policy and practice.
The Community Revitalization course emphasizes applied planning strategies aimed at strengthening communities, particularly in contexts experiencing social, economic, or physical challenges.
Students examine approaches to revitalization that address equity, economic development, housing, and the built environment.
The Planning Law course provides essential instruction in the legal frameworks that authorize and constrain planning practice.
Students learn how constitutional principles, statutes, and judicial decisions shape land use regulation, development review, and public decision-making, and how planners must integrate legal reasoning and ethical judgment into professional practice.
Together, these four courses provide a comprehensive preparation in social planning by linking planning theory, analytical methods, applied community interventions, and legal frameworks.
The certificate is designed to support students seeking professional planning knowledge applicable across public, nonprofit, and private-sector contexts.

The purpose of this proposal is to change the standing of the Physical Therapy Program from a program within the Kinesiology Department to a separate Department within the College of Human Science and Services. 8. 3 B.RATIONALE This organizational change is being proposed because the Physical Therapy Program can better fulfill its mission to educate competent doctors of physical therapy who can provide skilled patient care in a variety of settings, conduct clinical research, and provide service to the community at large if it is an academic department within the College of Human Science and Services rather than a program within the Kinesiology Department.
The mission of the Physical Therapy Program focuses on professional, graduate rather than undergraduate education as is the case in the Kinesiology Department.
There are no common students between the two units nor does faculty teach across the units.
The reorganization will allow PT faculty to focus their efforts on continued development and advancement of the program, clinical and basic science research related to the profession and provision of service to the community and profession.
The Physical Therapy Program has functioned autonomously within the (Department of Physical Education now renamed) Kinesiology Department since its inception in 1991.

It has had its own faculty, support staff, facilities, and budget from the very beginning as a requirement of professional accreditation.
Further, due to accreditation requirements, the Program Director has maintained direct communication with the Dean of the College and was a regular participant at College Management meetings.
A self-study report for the Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education was recently completed in preparation for a site visit that occurred in September 2005.
It was during this self- evaluation that the faculty recognized that the Program was intended to be a separate entity within the college from its development and that separation would allow for better overall functioning of the program.
With the recent move from the masters of physical therapy to the doctor of physical therapy, the program is even more out of place being located within the Kinesiology Department.
Separation will allow better collaboration between the Physical Therapy Program and other departments such as Communicative Disorders and Biology.
